study.title: Acts 11 - The entrance of the Gentiles, the growth in Antioch and the help of the brothers of Judea
study.overview: Acts 11 shows the church learning step by step not to resist the action of God among the Gentiles. Peter must explain why he entered the house of non-Jews and how the Holy Spirit confirmed that God was accepting those who believed in Jesus. Then the narrative turns to Antioch, where the gospel is also announced to the Greeks, many believe, Barnabas confirms the work, Saul is brought to teach, and the disciples first receive the name of Christians. The chapter ends with a prophecy of hunger and the practical response of the church, which decides to help the brothers of Judea through Barnabas and Saul.

outline.title: Questioning Peter in Jerusalem
outline.explanation: The brothers of Judea hear that Gentiles received the word of God and criticize Peter for having lived with uncircumcised. Peter then renders accounts in an orderly manner, showing that his attitude was not born on his own initiative, but of divine direction.

outline.title: Peter reports the divine vision and approval of the Gentiles
outline.explanation: Peter narrates the vision, the order of the Spirit, the preaching in the house of Cornelius and the descent of the Holy Spirit upon those Gentiles. The conclusion of the church is that God has also granted them repentance to life, and therefore one cannot resist what God does.

outline.title: The gospel reaches Antioch and the disciples are called Christians
outline.explanation: The scattered announce the word first to the Jews, but some also speak to the Greeks in Antioch. The Lord blesses the work, Barnabas sees the grace of God, calls Saul, and for a year both teach the multitude; there the disciples are named Christians.

outline.title: Prophecy of hunger and help to the brothers of Judea
outline.explanation: Prophets descend from Jerusalem, and Agabo announces a great famine. In response, the disciples organize themselves to send help as each one could, referring the offering to the elders through Barnabas and Saul.

study.context: The chapter reflects the clash between Jewish customs of social separation and the extension of the church to the Gentiles. According to the notes, the Jewish believers of Jerusalem stranged Peter's posture, because they associate and eat with Gentiles contradicted traditional practices. Also appears Antioch as an important center for missionary expansion, and the text highlights the dispersion caused by the persecution linked to Stephen. There is no need to resort to external information to realize that the chapter is dealing with the transition of the church's mission from a mostly Jewish environment to a work clearly aimed at non-Jews.
study.theology: The main emphasis of the chapter is that God takes the initiative in the inclusion of the Gentiles. Peter does not present his conduct as a human concession, but as submission to the will of God, confirmed by the gift of the Spirit. The church learns that salvation comes by faith in Christ and that God grants repentance to life to both Jews and Gentiles. The chapter also shows that God's work produces visible fruit: teaching, perseverance, Christian identity and concrete generosity. Communion between churches is not only doctrinal; it is also expressed in material care by the needy brothers and sisters. Barnabas appears as a model of encouragement, spiritual discernment and ministerial cooperation, while the elders emerge as responsible for receiving the help.

scholarViews.insight: The Jewish believers of Jerusalem criticized Peter because the Jews traditionally avoided social association with Gentiles; Peter responded by explaining that God himself had directed all that happened.
Peter explained in order that his entry into the house of Gentiles was the result of God's initiative, and that the Holy Spirit demonstrated that they were accepted and blessed by God.
Peter's answer emphasizes that God gave them the same gift, the Holy Spirit, and that no one could resist what God was doing.

questions: What does the reaction of the brothers of Jerusalem teach about how the church should deal with unexpected changes in God's work?
In what sense does the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Gentiles confirm that salvation is by God's initiative and not by ethnic barriers?
How can the generosity of the disciples of Antioch guide the way his church responds to the need for distant brothers?
study.practice: This chapter calls the church not to resist when God acts outside of our usual standards. In practice, this means hearing with humility, examining the work in the light of the gospel, and recognizing the fruits of the Spirit where Christ is truly announced. It also calls us to support missions and to care for brothers in need with organized generosity, as did the disciples of Antioch. A concrete application is to separate a regular contribution to Christian help and, at the same time, to cultivate a heart willing to welcome people different from us without prejudice.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not definitively clarify who exactly were the elders mentioned in verse 30; Adam Clarke presents possibilities, but this remains interpretive. There are also details about Antioch and about the prophets who come from Jerusalem that the notes deal generally, without accurate identification of names beyond Agabo. Therefore, any more specific statement on these points would require caution beyond the material provided.
